**Separate the decision to spend from the amount spent after that decision.** A single continuous regression can struggle when 80% of outcomes are exactly zero and the rest follow a long positive tail. A hurdle model uses a gate for positive outcome and a second model for positive magnitude. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

If purchase probability is 0.2 and mean positive spend is 50, expected spend is 10. The two components can depend on different features: one may predict willingness to buy, another basket size among buyers.

**Zero-inflated and hurdle models are not identical.** In a hurdle model, the positive component cannot generate zero. In a zero-inflated count model, a structural-zero component is mixed with a count distribution that can also produce zero. Choose according to how the data arise.

Evaluate gate calibration and positive-tail fit separately before evaluating aggregate value. For a log-normal positive component, exponentiating its mean log spend is not its arithmetic mean. Also check observation windows: a customer who has not purchased yet may be censored rather than a permanent zero.

**Technical details and references.**

A hurdle model first predicts whether the outcome is positive, then models its positive magnitude. For the example, use a Bernoulli purchase/spend gate and a positive distribution such as log-normal. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

$$E[Y\mid x]=P(Y>0\mid x)E[Y\mid Y>0,x].$$

Zero-inflated count models instead mix a structural-zero process with a count distribution that can also generate zero; that differs from a hurdle's zero-truncated positive component. Select the model from how zeros arise, not their frequency alone. Evaluate gate calibration, positive-tail fit, and aggregate value. Delayed purchases may be censored rather than permanent zeros.
